## The idea

Pitch has two kinds of location. MIDI note 60 identifies one particular C, while the label C also connects that note to all the other Cs above and below it. One representation keeps register; the other treats octave-related pitches as members of the same family.

Walk from MIDI 60 to 72 in semitone steps and the distinction becomes audible. The program triggers thirteen notes across twelve rises, and the final sound resembles the first in a higher register. A *pitch class* keeps position within this repeating twelve-step cycle and discards octave information. In code, `pitch % 12` performs that reduction. MIDI notes 36, 60, and 84 are different addresses, yet all produce pitch class 0.

The keyboard makes the cycle navigable through its uneven groups of black keys. Those visual landmarks do not change the equal semitone spacing, but they help you locate a class inside the recurring pattern.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 120
use_synth :piano

define :pitch_class do |pitch|
  pitch % 12
end

(60..72).each do |pitch|
  play pitch, release: 0.15
  puts "pitch #{pitch}, class #{pitch_class(pitch)}"
  sleep 0.25
end

sleep 1
(36..84).select { |pitch| pitch_class(pitch) == 0 }.each do |pitch|
  play pitch, release: 0.4
  sleep 0.5
end
```

The first pass rises through all twelve chromatic classes and reaches the starting class again at 72. Watch the printed class values run from 0 through 11 and wrap to 0 while the MIDI address continues upward. The second pass filters a much wider range for class 0. You hear separated Cs rather than adjacent notes, each twelve semitones from the next.

## Change one thing

1. Change the selected class from `0` to `7`. The second pass now finds every G. Its MIDI values differ from the Cs, but the twelve-semitone spacing between successive results remains unchanged.

2. Restore class 0, then start the chromatic walk at 61. The class sequence now begins at 1 and returns there at 73. You have rotated the cycle without changing its length or direction.

3. Restore the original range and increase each chromatic sleep to `0.5`. Trace the notes on a keyboard diagram or controller as they sound. The slower rate gives the black-key landmarks time to register.

## Why it works

Modulo maps an integer address onto a repeating range. Dividing a MIDI note by twelve leaves a remainder from 0 through 11, and notes separated by twelve share that remainder. The operation is familiar from a circular buffer or clock face: the full count continues, while the position within the cycle repeats.

This reduction is useful because many musical operations care about note identity apart from register. A chord analyser may want to know that several notes include class 0, regardless of which C each instrument plays. Transposition can add a fixed amount and reduce modulo twelve to remain within the class set.

The lost information is equally important. Once 48, 60, and 72 have all become 0, no calculation can recover which octave supplied the original. A renderer cannot play “pitch class 0” until you choose a register. Keep the full MIDI address whenever height, range, voicing, or physical frequency remains part of the question.

The conventional numeric mapping places C at class 0 because C4 has MIDI address 60 and `60 % 12` is 0. Other interfaces may display names instead of integers or begin their lists elsewhere. The underlying cycle still contains twelve positions. State the convention at a program boundary, compare numeric classes internally, and attach a display name when a person needs one.

The printed output lets you inspect both coordinate systems at once. If the sound reaches an octave but the class does not wrap, the modulo operation is wrong. If the class wraps correctly but playback lands in the wrong register, the lost octave information was used where a full address belonged.

Lesson 9 makes register the variable and therefore retains the complete MIDI addresses. Lesson 10 adds another layer that modulo also erases: two different spellings can refer to the same sounding class while describing different musical motion.

## Take it further

Write a chromatic browser with variables named `start` and `offset`. For offsets 0 through 12, play `start + offset` and print both its full MIDI address and its pitch class. The thirteen printed rows should show a complete cycle whose first and last entries share a class.

Add a second pass that searches MIDI 36 through 84 for one chosen class. Print each matching address before playing it. Check the arithmetic in the log, then audition both passes in Sonic Pi 5: the chromatic browser should move by semitone, while the filtered notes should move by octaves. Those different sounds arise from two views of the same integer space.
